one_liner: Single-threaded io_uring key-value cache server in C; README claims 7x Redis and 46x memcached GET throughput at 16 B.
what_it_does: A standalone in-memory cache server (about 1,000 lines of C) that stores byte-string keys and values in fixed 16 MB blocks and evicts the oldest block when memory or the fixed-size index fills (FIFO). Clients speak its own little-endian binary TCP protocol with four commands, get, set, getz and setz (zstd-compressed set/get), plus a stat dump; set sends no reply and a miss returns a zero length. It is not a Redis or memcached replacement: there is no DEL, TTL, data types, persistence, auth or replication, and the only published client is the author's Python asyncio package (asyncmrcache). Its PyPI release (0.2, June 2020) predates getz/setz, which were added on the client's GitHub master in March 2024.
how_it_is_fast: Networking uses io_uring with SQPOLL, multishot accept and multishot recv into a 16,384-entry provided buffer ring, and the event loop busy-polls the completion ring, so the user thread makes almost no syscalls and the kernel's SQ thread does the submission work on another core. Every request in a received chunk is parsed in place and all replies go out in one writev whose iovecs point straight at the stored item (length header plus value), so GET replies are never copied in user space. Lookup is wyhash plus linear probing in a power-of-two table of 8-byte slots that pack a 28-bit block id, 12 hash bits and a 24-bit offset; a SET is a bump allocation into the current block and eviction drops a whole block, so there is no per-item free or LRU bookkeeping.
when_to_use: Studying or forking a compact io_uring server: SQPOLL, multishot accept/recv, provided buffer rings and one zero-copy writev per received chunk, all in a few hundred lines of net.c.

A trusted, single-tenant cache of many small items behind your own client, where about 18 B of per-item overhead (8 B index slot at a 70% load cap plus a 6 B item header) matters more than Redis features and FIFO eviction is acceptable.
Read-heavy, pipelined GET traffic from a few long-lived connections on one Linux 6.0+ machine, where giving up one spinning user core plus the SQPOLL kernel core is acceptable.
Large compressible values you want stored zstd-compressed (level 2) on the server via setz/getz, trading GET throughput (979k to 212k ops/s at 10 kB in the README) for RAM.
when_not_to_use: You need Redis or memcached protocol compatibility, data types, TTLs, DEL, persistence, replication or auth; none exist, and set has no acknowledgement.

Clients are untrusted, buggy or reconnect often: request lengths are not validated, an unknown command frees the connection while its multishot recv is still armed, and client sockets are never closed.

Memory beyond the item store is tight: the receive pool is 16,384 x 32 KB = 512 MB of address space (each buffer gets at least one page touched as the ring cycles, so 64 MB or more resident), each connection callocs about 6.3 MB of iovec groups, and the index is sized once at startup and never grows.
You want multi-core scaling or an idle server that sleeps: there is one event-loop thread, and it spins on the completion ring even with no traffic.
Kernel older than 6.0 or any non-Linux platform: IORING_SETUP_SINGLE_ISSUER and multishot recv need 6.0, although the README says 5.5+ in one place and 5.8+ in another.

integration.form: source-drop (standalone server binary; clients use its binary TCP protocol)
integration.dependencies: liburing (provided-buffer-ring API, io_uring_setup_buf_ring) and libzstd; wyhash.h is vendored. The Makefile also links -lmrloop, which the source no longer uses.
integration.min_toolchain: gcc with -std=c99 -D_GNU_SOURCE (the repo's bld script uses -O3); Linux kernel 6.0+ in practice
integration.platforms: Linux only (io_uring); the parser does native-endian unaligned loads, so little-endian x86-64 or aarch64
integration.thread_safety: Single-threaded server: one event-loop thread plus the kernel SQPOLL thread, with no locks and no multi-core scaling.

gotchas: Harness flaw (bench/bench.go): the client counts a batch as done after length*batch reply bytes, read in 4 KB chunks, but mrcache sends 4+length bytes per GET and Redis 23 bytes at 16 B. Once a batch's replies exceed one 4 KB read (batch above about 200 at 16 B), leftover reply bytes carry into the next batch and, at many batch sizes, keep piling up, so the client stops waiting for its own batch. The reported rate then tends to 1.25x the served rate for mrcache and 1.44x for Redis at 16 B, so this bias favours Redis rather than mrcache. The zstd row used an all-zero 10 kB value (rand.Read is commented out), which is zstd's best case.

The server cannot safely absorb deep pipelines. Each received chunk (up to 32 KB) is answered with one writev from a fixed 1,024-entry iovec array with no bounds check, so more than 1,024 GETs in one chunk (about 20 KB of 16-byte-key GETs) overflows into the free list and the next iovec group and exceeds IOV_MAX. In addition, a short write that ends inside the first iovec resends that whole iovec and desyncs the stream.

No input validation: SET value lengths (signed 32-bit) are never checked against the 16 MB block size, so an oversized or negative length writes past the block. GETZ on a key stored with plain SET tests an unsigned ZSTD_getFrameContentSize result with `< 0`, so the guard never fires: the server mallocs 2 bytes, writes a 4-byte header into them and queues a negative-length reply, and the client gets no answer. A SETZ whose compression fails (for example, an incompressible value above about 2 MB overflowing the vlen+64 output buffer) never advances the parse pointer, so the single thread spins forever. GETZ decompression buffers are also stored at free_me[num] instead of free_me[num-1], so the last buffer of every write leaks; with one GETZ per write, every buffer leaks.

Connections leak. No close() appears anywhere in the server, and an EOF completion arrives without IORING_CQE_F_MORE, so it falls into the write-completion branch and free_conn never runs. Each closed client therefore leaks its fd and its roughly 6.3 MB connection struct. The README's `make` fails: the Makefile wildcard also compiles probe.c, which has its own main(), and it links the dropped -lmrloop; use the bld script instead. The documented -z/--zstd flag is not parsed (it prints usage and exits with status 2), and the default -m is 128 MB, not the 256 MB the README and usage text state.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Pogocache, Dragonfly or Valkey when you need a drop-in Redis/Memcached server with published versions and repeatable runs (Pogocache: about 2.0x Redis 8.2.1 GET at pipeline 1, median of 31 runs). Pick mrcache only when you control both client and server, want the lowest per-item overhead for many small items on one core with FIFO eviction, or want a small io_uring server to study or fork and harden.
verified_claims_summary: The README reports single-node GET throughput from the repo's Go client (bench.go, localhost by default), which fetches one zero-filled 16-byte key over and over: 18.6m ops/s against Redis 2.5m and memcached 400k with 16 B values, and 979k against 313k and 261k with 10 kB values (212k with zstd on an all-zero value). No CPU, kernel, compiler, Redis or memcached version or configuration, connection count or batch size is given, and the memcached client is not in the repo. mrcache's numbers come from a busy-polling event thread plus an SQPOLL kernel thread, while the Redis and memcached configurations are unstated.
status_note: Stale: last commit 2024-10-29, last code change 2024-05-12, and issue #2 (2020) is still open. MIT and small enough to read in an afternoon, but experimental code: the connection leak, unchecked request lengths and the 1,024-iovec limit make it unfit for production without fixes, and it should be built with the bld script rather than make.
